In [[geometry]], a '''diminished trapezohedron''' is a [[polyhedron]] in an infinite set of polyhedra, constructed by removing one of the polar vertices of a [[trapezohedron]] and replacing it by a new face ([[Diminishment (geometry)|diminishment]]). It has one regular {{nowrap|{{mvar|n}}-gonal}} base face, {{mvar|n}} [[triangle]] faces around the base, and {{mvar|n}} [[kite (geometry)|kite]]s meeting on top. The kites can also be replaced by [[rhombi]] with specific proportions.

Along with the set of [[pyramid (geometry)|pyramids]] and [[elongated pyramid]]s, these figures are topologically [[Self-dual polyhedron|self-dual]].

It can also be seen as an augmented {{nowrap|{{mvar|n}}-gonal}} [[antiprism]], with a {{nowrap|{{mvar|n}}-gonal}} pyramid augmented onto one of the {{nowrap|{{mvar|n}}-gonal}} faces, and whose height is adjusted so the upper antiprism triangle faces can be made coparallel to the pyramid faces and merged into kite-shaped faces.

They're also related to the [[gyroelongated pyramid]]s, as augmented antiprisms and which are Johnson solids for {{math|1=''n'' = 4, 5}}. This sequence has sets of two triangles instead of kite faces.

== Special cases ==

There are three special case geometries of the ''diminished trigonal trapezohedron''. The simplest is a '''diminished cube'''. The '''Chestahedron''', named after artist [[Frank Chester (artist)|Frank Chester]], is constructed with equilateral triangles around the base, and the geometry adjusted so the kite faces have the same area as the equilateral triangles.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://frankchester.com/chestahedron-geometry/|title=Chestahedron Geometry|website=The Art & Science of Frank Chester|language=en-US|access-date=2020-01-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://demonstrations.wolfram.com/TransformingATetrahedronIntoAChestahedron/|title=Transforming a Tetrahedron into a Chestahedron|last=Donke|first=Hans-Joakim|date=March 2011|website=Wolfram Alpha|url-status=live|access-date=22 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141007023603/http://demonstrations.wolfram.com/TransformingATetrahedronIntoAChestahedron/ |archive-date=2014-10-07 }}</ref> The last can be seen by [[Augmentation (geometry)|augmenting]] a regular [[tetrahedron]] and an [[octahedron]], leaving 10 equilateral triangle faces, and then merging 3 sets of coparallel equilateral triangular faces into 3 (60 degree) rhombic faces. It can also be seen as a tetrahedron with 3 of 4 of its vertices [[Rectification (geometry)|rectified]].  The three rhombic faces fold out flat to form half of a [[hexagram]].
